title: Your SIN, CRA My Account & Getting Paid in Canada
summary: Learn what a SIN is for, how to protect it, and the official paths for CRA My Account and direct deposit.

introHtml:
Learn what a SIN is for, how to protect it, and the official paths for CRA My Account and direct deposit.

Learners can explain what a SIN is for, list safer ways to protect it, describe what CRA My Account is (at a high level), and know official paths to set up direct deposit for CRA payments — without treating this course as personal tax help.
certificateNote: It is not a college diploma, degree, trade ticket, professional licence, or immigration, legal, tax, or financial advice.

lessons.title: What is a Social Insurance Number (SIN)?
lessons.html:
A Social Insurance Number (SIN) is a 9-digit number used in Canada for work and for many government programs and benefits. Service Canada explains that your SIN is private, and it is illegal for someone else to use it.

You may need a SIN to:

  • work for an employer who must report your income
  • file taxes and receive certain benefits
  • deal with some financial accounts that must report interest or income

Service Canada no longer issues new plastic SIN cards. Older plastic cards can still be used. If you need to see your number, you can often find it on tax slips (such as a T4), on a past tax return, or by signing in to My Service Canada Account (MSCA).

Your SIN is not a general ID card. Do not use it like a driver’s licence or passport when a business only wants ID.

If you are new to Canada, the steps to apply can depend on your status. This course will not tell you which immigration category you are in. Use the official SIN pages on Canada.ca and get help from a settlement or adult learning worker if you need support filling forms.

lessons.title: Protect your SIN
lessons.html:
If the wrong person gets your SIN, they may try identity fraud — for example opening accounts or filing false information in your name. Service Canada’s protection guidance says to limit who has access.

Safer habits:

  • Do not carry your SIN card or confirmation letter every day if you do not need it.
  • Store papers with your SIN in a safe place; shred them before throwing them out.
  • Share your SIN only when it is required (for example, after you are hired for payroll, or with a bank when the law requires tax reporting).
  • Never give your SIN in a surprise phone call, text, or email from someone you did not contact.

You are often not required to give a SIN for things like a job application before hiring, renting many apartments, a credit card application, or phone/internet signup (there are limited exceptions described on Canada.ca). If a business asks and it is not required by law, you can ask why, offer other ID, and refuse.

Scam warning: Messages that say your SIN is “cancelled,” or that ask you to “verify your SIN” by clicking a link, are suspicious. Hang up or delete. Use official websites you type yourself.

If you think your SIN was stolen or misused, follow the official “fraud and data breaches” guidance on Canada.ca and report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre as needed.

lessons.title: What is CRA My Account?
lessons.html:
My Account is the Canada Revenue Agency’s online portal for individuals. Inside your CRA account you can view tax and benefit information after you register and verify your identity.

Public CRA pages explain that to use My Account you generally need:

  • a Social Insurance Number, and
  • a filed and assessed income tax and benefit return from the current or previous tax year

Sign-in options can include a CRA user ID and password, a Sign-In Partner (online banking), or some provincial partners (for example an Alberta.ca Account where available). Details change — always follow the current canada.ca steps.

What people often use it for (overview only): viewing notices, checking benefit-related information, updating some profile details, and managing direct deposit for CRA payments once you have full access. Some features need finished identity verification.

Safety: Bookmark the official sign-in path (for example canada.ca/my-cra-account style addresses that stay on canada.ca). Do not sign in through a link in a surprise email.

This lesson does not teach you how to complete a tax return. If you need filing help, ask your council about community tax clinics or trusted preparers.

lessons.title: Direct deposit for CRA payments
lessons.html:
Direct deposit means the CRA puts refunds or benefit payments into your Canadian bank or credit union account instead of mailing a cheque. CRA pages say you can set this up through your CRA account or through many Canadian banks and credit unions.

Important points from public CRA guidance:

  • Direct deposit is for Canadian bank or credit union accounts.
  • You can no longer start or update CRA direct deposit by telephone.
  • Online updates through your CRA account or participating bank are usually faster (CRA describes next-business-day updates after consent in many cases).
  • Mail-in enrolment is possible if you cannot use online methods, but it can take much longer (CRA estimates up to about three months or more).
  • Do not close an old account until you see a payment arrive in the new one.

High-level CRA account path (confirm on the live page): sign in → Individual / My Account → Profile → Direct deposit → Edit.

Not the same system: CPP, OAS, and EI have their own government direct-deposit processes. The CRA page notes it does not administer those programs.

Again: this is not personal financial advice. If a payment is missing, use official CRA contact options after waiting the timeframes they publish.

lessons.title: Getting paid at work and staying safe
lessons.html:
When you work in Canada, employers generally need your SIN after you are hired so they can report income. You should receive pay stubs and, each year, tax slips such as a T4. Keep those documents for your records.

Pay methods vary by employer: direct deposit to your bank is common; some still use cheques. Ask your employer’s payroll office how you get paid and how to update your bank info through them — that is separate from CRA benefit direct deposit.

Red flags:

  • An “employer” asks for your SIN, banking password, or e-Transfer before you have a real job offer and paperwork.
  • Someone asks you to “cash a cheque and send money back.”
  • A surprise message claims the CRA needs your payroll password.

Use official SIN protection habits. For workplace problems (unpaid wages, unfair treatment), this course cannot give legal advice — ask your council about employment standards referrals in Alberta or elsewhere.

Practice task (offline): Write three places you would store pay stubs safely, and one person you could ask at your council if a job offer feels like a scam.
